title: Cruise Ship Emissions Raise Virus Risks at Ports
paragraphs: Cruise holidays have become increasingly popular, and many port cities welcome thousands of passengers every day. However, a new study suggests that the air pollution produced by cruise ships in ports could make people more vulnerable to viral infections such as the common cold and COVID-19.

The study, which was published in July 2026 in the journal Environment International, was carried out by researchers at the University of Southampton in the UK. Southampton is one of Britain's busiest cruise ports. The researchers collected air samples at five locations around the port, including a busy cruise terminal, a container ship terminal and a gate used by trucks. They also collected samples at a site about five kilometers from the port for comparison. Samples were taken in late spring and early summer, and the cruise terminal was also sampled in winter, when far fewer cruise ships visit.

The researchers focused on ultrafine particles, tiny pieces of pollution that can travel deep into the lungs and may even enter the bloodstream. According to the study, these particles are essentially unregulated and generally not monitored. At the cruise terminal, the particles contained higher levels of metals, including vanadium and nickel, in summer than in winter. Levels were also higher when the wind blew from the direction of the cruise ships and when more ships were present, which suggested that the pollution came from ships burning fuel.

In laboratory experiments, the researchers exposed human lung cells to the particles. They found that the particles increased inflammation and reduced the activity of genes that help the body defend itself against viruses. Moreover, vanadium increased the number of copies of both viruses tested. Professor Matthew Loxham, the study's senior author, said that this "has potential implications for the severity and spread of infection."

However, the researchers acknowledge that the experiments show that the effect is biologically possible, rather than directly measuring illness in real people. Nevertheless, they recommend reducing ship emissions near populated areas, for example by allowing ships to plug into clean electricity while they are docked.
